executive_summary: The defining thread of today's content is the intensifying battle over who controls the future of artificial intelligence, a contest playing out simultaneously in courtrooms, corporate strategy, and public infrastructure. The MIT Technology Review's two-piece coverage of the Musk v. Altman trial lays bare how the AI race has become a raw power struggle — the case collapsed not because OpenAI was absolved of betraying its nonprofit mission, but on a procedural technicality, leaving the deeper question of corporate accountability in AI unresolved and consequential. Google's position entering I/O 2026 as a third-place foundation model competitor further illustrates that the AI hierarchy is rapidly consolidating, with real strategic losers emerging. The Economist's newsletter question — whether the backlash against data centers is justified — connects directly to this theme, since the physical infrastructure underpinning AI dominance is itself becoming a geopolitical and environmental flashpoint. Taken together, today's content makes clear that the AI power struggle has matured from a story about innovation into one about control: of compute, of capital, of narrative, and of the institutional rules that govern all three.

newsletters.title: The Morning: The race to control Congress

items.headline: Map quests
items.blurb: History tells us that the party in power generally loses congressional seats in midterm elections. Yesterday's New York Times/Siena poll showed that Democrats should be in a good position to pick some up. Democrats had an 11-point lead when registered voters were asked which party's candidate they would support for Congress — well ahead of where voters ranked Democrats earlier in this cycle, writes Nate Cohn, our chief political analyst. Currently, Republicans hold narrow majorities in both the House and the Senate. Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and four seats in the Senate to flip control of Congress. And polling is an important bellwether for their chances. But congressional maps can confound voter sentiment and polarize races, as these charts from my colleague Ashley Wu show. For Democrats in particular, they pose a problem. A month ago, the party expected a blue wave. Then the Supreme Court said a new congressional map in Louisiana, drawn to protect Black representation in Congress, was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. After that, Republican-led states across the South went to work. Louisiana is crafting a new map. Florida drew one aimed at getting rid of four seats that leaned toward Democrats. Tennessee designed one that would give Republicans an additional seat. Voters in California and Virginia opted to go in the other direction, authorizing their leaders to draw maps that would create new Democratic seats. The Supreme Court in Virginia threw out that state's measure — and four seats for the left — early this month.

items.headline: The Trump loyalty test
items.blurb: One race to watch closely today is the Republican primary in Kentucky, where Representative Thomas Massie, who has clashed with President Trump, is trying to keep his seat against Ed Gallrein, a challenger backed by the president. Kentucky has an unpredictable political landscape, Reid Epstein reported. It's a deep-red state with a Democratic governor. One of its senators is an insider's insider, Mitch McConnell, who is retiring. The other is Rand Paul, an outsider libertarian. Ever since Daniel Boone crossed the Cumberland Gap into what is now Kentucky, the state has served as an incubator for colorful figures who stand out for their quirks, their rejection of party orthodoxy and their national success despite long odds. Massie and Gallrein fit right into that tradition. Will voters prefer their incumbent — a libertarian-leaning maverick — or vote instead for a MAGA-aligned former Navy SEAL with a huge war chest and no experience in holding office? (Yesterday, in an unusual move, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Kentucky to stump for Gallrein.)

newsletters.title: The best NBA game of the decade?

items.headline: Just … how, Wemby?
items.blurb: Nothing said about Victor Wembanyama today will qualify as hyperbole. That's how good he was in San Antonio's 122-115 double-overtime win in Oklahoma City, which probably qualifies as one of the best NBA playoff games of the last decade. Wembanyama scored 41 points and grabbed 24 rebounds in the win, which gives the Spurs a 1-0 lead in the Western Conference finals over the defending champs.

items.headline: The Habs, away from home
items.blurb: The barn in Buffalo looked incredible for last night's Game 7 between the Canadiens and Sabres, particularly as the game wore on. Montreal took an early 2-0 lead in the first period, but that melted to a 2-2 tie in the third. KeyBank Center was frothy. Montreal held, and overtime arrived. Then Alex Newhook happened 11:22 into OT. The Canadiens advance to the Eastern Conference final for the first time since 2021 and get there via two consecutive Game 7 road wins.

items.headline: The PWHL handled business in regulation — barely
items.blurb: Like their city mates, the Montreal Victoire had a chance to close out a series last night, but this was for a title, and the Victoire were 5:30 away from a clean sweep of the Walter Cup Finals. As if they drew it up in a kid's backyard dream, the Ottawa Charge scored two goals in that final 5:30 to turn a 1-0 deficit into a 2-1 lead. Ottawa saved its season and prevented Montreal from celebrating on its ice. Game 4 is Wednesday in Ottawa.

items.headline: Sorsby sues NCAA
items.blurb: As expected, Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby sued the NCAA to reinstate his eligibility for the upcoming season while he is under investigation for gambling violations. In his affidavit, Sorsby admitted to betting on Indiana while he was a reserve on the Hoosiers roster, and he is ultimately seeking a quick decision so he can apply to the NFL's supplemental draft in June if his college career is done. What a mess.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Here’s why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI
longform.thesis: Elon Musk lost his lawsuit against OpenAI not on the merits of whether the company betrayed its nonprofit mission, but because the jury found he filed too late under statutes of limitations.
longform.context: A jury returned a verdict in Musk's suit against OpenAI, which he had brought claiming the company breached its founding contract as a nonprofit by shifting toward a for-profit structure — a case that became a high-profile proxy battle over OpenAI's governance and direction.
arguments: The verdict was procedural, not substantive: the jury determined Musk's claims were time-barred, meaning the court never adjudicated whether OpenAI actually violated its nonprofit mission.

The central factual dispute was temporal: OpenAI argued the for-profit shift was visible as early as 2017, which would place Musk's 2022 discovery claim well outside the limitations window, while Musk maintained he only became aware of the structural change in 2022.

Despite the loss, the piece signals the underlying governance fight is unresolved — the article notes 'the fight over OpenAI's structure may not be over,' suggesting further legal or regulatory challenges remain possible.
longform.significance: The verdict leaves OpenAI's nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion legally unscrutinized on the merits, allowing the company to continue its structural transition without a judicial ruling on whether it breached its founding obligations. This matters at a moment when OpenAI is completing a full for-profit conversion worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and when questions about AI lab accountability and mission drift are intensifying across the industry. The outcome also illustrates how procedural law can shield consequential institutional decisions from substantive public accountability.
questions_raised: Since the jury ruled only on timing and not on whether OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission, what legal or regulatory avenue — if any — could force a merits-based adjudication of that founding contract?

If OpenAI's for-profit shift was legally visible as early as 2017, what does that imply about the adequacy of oversight by the company's board, state attorneys general, and other fiduciaries during the intervening years?

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two competing narratives: Altman as a self-dealing liar and Musk as a power-hungry AGI monopolist.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch covers week three of the ongoing civil trial between Elon Musk and Sam Altman over OpenAI's contested nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, filed by reporter-lawyer Michelle Kim who attended proceedings in person.
arguments: Musk's legal team framed Altman as dishonest and conflicted, accusing him of 'lying and self-dealing' in his stewardship of OpenAI, attacking his personal credibility as the foundation of the plaintiff's case.

Altman's defense countered by portraying Musk as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence,' reframing the lawsuit not as principled mission-protection but as a strategic bid to dominate AGI development.

The trial surfaced new documentary and testimonial evidence about OpenAI's nonprofit status and internal culture, including a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk,' suggesting a pattern of retaliatory behavior that undermines Musk's stated altruistic motives.
longform.significance: The verdict will establish a legal and reputational precedent for how AGI-focused organizations can transition from nonprofit to commercial structures, a question with industry-wide consequences. The trial also forces a public reckoning with whether Silicon Valley's most powerful AI actors are motivated by safety or self-interest. With jury deliberations now beginning, the outcome could materially affect OpenAI's ongoing restructuring and Musk's parallel AGI venture xAI.
questions_raised: Whether the jury's credibility determination — Altman as fraudulent versus Musk as power-hungry — will turn on documentary evidence or personal testimony, and whether either framing is legally sufficient to adjudicate the nonprofit conversion dispute.

What the trial's disclosure that xAI 'distills OpenAI's models' (surfaced in week one) means for Musk's standing as a plaintiff claiming mission betrayal, given his company may have commercially exploited the very IP at issue.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place competitor in foundation models, with a critical coding deficit against Anthropic and OpenAI but a defensible lead in AI for science — and its conference announcements must be evaluated against both realities.
longform.context: The piece is a pre-conference preview written ahead of Google I/O 2026, prompted by a sharp shift in Google's competitive standing since I/O 2025, when the company still appeared roughly co-equal with its rivals following the strong launch of Gemini 2.5 Pro.
arguments: Google has fallen to third place in the foundation model race primarily because its coding tools have been 'outgunned' by Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex — a deficit so severe that DeepMind engineers were reportedly allowed to use Claude for internal work, a striking signal of product failure from within.

Google is mounting a coding comeback through a new DeepMind coding team and the involvement of Nobel laureate John Jumper, likely to produce a major release — possibly an update to the 'Antigravity' agentic coding platform — but the author judges transformative progress implausible given that internal users were 'still reportedly fighting over who got access to Claude Code last month.'

Science and health remain Google's 'conspicuous strength,' with tools like the AI co-scientist (called an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve representing genuine frontier work, though the forthcoming Health Coach appears limited to fitness and diet advice rather than clinical concerns, raising the question of whether this reflects competitive lag or 'appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain.'

Google faces internal political pressure — 600 employees, many from DeepMind, protested a DoD contract that Pichai signed the following day — and must navigate this controversy alongside the spectacle of the Musk v. Altman trial occurring 30 miles away, testing whether 'Google can maintain its veneer of neutrality.'
longform.significance: The piece matters because it frames Google I/O 2026 not as a product showcase but as a competitive stress test, forcing a distinction between domains where Google leads (scientific AI) and where it has structurally fallen behind (coding). It also surfaces the underreported tension between Google's research credibility — anchored by a Nobel Prize — and its failure to translate that into market-leading developer tools, a gap that has direct consequences for enterprise adoption.
questions_raised: Whether Google's restraint in health AI (a consumer-facing Health Coach focused on fitness rather than medicine) represents strategic caution or an inability to compete with OpenAI's more aggressive clinical positioning — the author raises this directly but leaves it unresolved.

Whether the internal employee protest over the DoD deal signals a deeper cultural fracture at DeepMind that could constrain Google's ability to pursue government and defense contracts that rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic are actively winning.
